questions.question: Explain the four Spring Batch parallelism strategies — multi-threaded step, parallel steps, async processor/writer, and partitioning (local/remote).
questions.title: Spring Batch Parallelism: Multi-Threaded, Async, Partitioning
questions.direct_answer: Spring Batch has four parallelism strategies. **Multi-threaded step** runs one step on multiple threads sharing the reader/writer (reader must be thread-safe; restart weakens). **Parallel steps** run independent steps concurrently via a `split` in the job flow. **Async processor/writer** wraps each item in a `Future` on a thread pool — best when the **processor is I/O-bound**. **Partitioning** splits input into ranges; a master step launches N worker steps locally or on remote JVMs via messaging — scales best and preserves restartability per slice. Choose based on where the bottleneck is: CPU (partitioning / multi-threaded), per-item I/O (async), independent workloads (parallel steps).

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using multi-threaded step with non-thread-safe reader; partitioning when a simpler strategy would work

sections.title: Why Parallelism — Map the Bottleneck to the Right Strategy
sections.content:
Single-threaded Spring Batch steps bottleneck on **per-item I/O** (external API per record), **CPU work** on large datasets, **DB throughput** (single connection serializes inserts), or **independent workloads** the job could run concurrently. The four parallelism strategies map to these bottlenecks differently — picking the wrong one wastes complexity without solving the problem.

**The four strategies in order of complexity:**
- **Multi-threaded step** — one step, multiple threads share reader/writer
- **Parallel steps** — independent steps run concurrently via `split`
- **Async processor/writer** — `AsyncItemProcessor` / `AsyncItemWriter` execute per-item processing on a thread pool
- **Partitioning (local or remote)** — master step splits input; N worker steps process slices independently

**Decision principle:**
- Bottleneck is processor I/O per item → **async processor/writer**
- Independent unrelated work → **parallel steps**
- Huge dataset that splits naturally by key → **partitioning**
- Simple single-machine throughput, restart not critical → **multi-threaded step**
- Otherwise → stay single-threaded and tune chunk size + writer choice first

sections.title: Master + Worker Topology for Partitioning
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    job["Job: nightlyReport"]
    job --> masterStep["Master Step (partitioner+handler)"]
    masterStep --> partitioner["Partitioner: split input into N slices (e.g., hash(customerId) mod N)"]
    partitioner --> ctx1["ExecutionContext slice 1 (minId=0, maxId=100K)"]
    partitioner --> ctx2["ExecutionContext slice 2 (minId=100K, maxId=200K)"]
    partitioner --> ctxN["ExecutionContext slice N (minId=900K, maxId=1M)"]
    ctx1 --> worker1["Worker Step 1 (reader+processor+writer)"]
    ctx2 --> worker2["Worker Step 2 (reader+processor+writer)"]
    ctxN --> workerN["Worker Step N (reader+processor+writer)"]
    worker1 --> repo[("JobRepository (StepExecution per worker)")]
    worker2 --> repo
    workerN --> repo
    masterStep -.coordinates via.-> handler["PartitionHandler (TaskExecutor or MessageChannel)"]
    handler -.local.-> threadPool["ThreadPoolTaskExecutor (in-JVM workers)"]
    handler -.remote.-> queue["Message Channel (Kafka, AMQP, JMS)"]
    queue --> remoteWorker1["Remote Worker JVM 1"]
    queue --> remoteWorkerM["Remote Worker JVM M"]
```

sections.title: Strategy 1 — Multi-Threaded Step
Strategy 2 — Parallel Steps via Split Flow
sections.content:
Multiple independent steps run concurrently using a `TaskExecutor`. The split joins all branches before the next step runs.

```java
@Bean
public Job importJob(JobRepository repo,
                     Step loadCustomers, Step loadProducts, Step loadOrders,
                     Step aggregate, TaskExecutor taskExecutor) {
    Flow loadAll = new FlowBuilder<SimpleFlow>("loadAll")
            .split(taskExecutor)
            .add(
                new FlowBuilder<SimpleFlow>("custFlow").start(loadCustomers).build(),
                new FlowBuilder<SimpleFlow>("prodFlow").start(loadProducts).build(),
                new FlowBuilder<SimpleFlow>("ordFlow").start(loadOrders).build())
            .build();

    return new JobBuilder("importJob", repo)
            .start(loadAll)
            .next(aggregate)
            .build();
}
```

**Behavior**
- Each step has its own reader/writer — no thread-safety issues
- Each step has independent restart state — failed branches restart independently
- The aggregate step waits for all branches to complete

**Use when**
- Genuinely independent workloads (load three reference tables before main processing)
- Wall-clock matters and the workloads have no data dependency

**Pitfalls**
- **Hidden data dependencies** — flows that share a target table can deadlock
- **Single-thread executor** — silent serialization
- **Long-tail flow blocking the join** — one slow flow holds back the next step

sections.title: Strategy 3 — Async Processor and Writer
Strategy 4 — Partitioning (Local and Remote)
Strategy Comparison
sections.content:
Pick the simplest strategy that fits the bottleneck.

| Strategy | Best For | Restart Semantics | Thread-Safety Requirement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Multi-threaded step | Simple I/O-bound step on one machine | Weak; reader position imprecise | Reader must be wrapped (`SynchronizedItemStreamReader`) |
| Parallel steps (split) | Independent workloads in DAG | Strong; each step independent | None (each step has its own reader/writer) |
| Async processor/writer | Per-item I/O-bound (HTTP, lookups) | Normal (reader serial) | Processor outputs must be thread-safe |
| Partitioning (local) | Large datasets, in-JVM scaling | Strong; per-partition restart | None (each worker has its own reader/writer) |
| Partitioning (remote) | Massive datasets, cluster scaling | Strong; per-partition restart | None; messaging coordinates |

sections.title: Choosing a Strategy and the Pitfalls That Follow
sections.content:
**When parallelism helps:**
- Bottleneck identified by measurement, not theory
- Datasets large enough that wall-clock saving justifies complexity
- Idempotent processors and writers ready for re-execution under restart

**When parallelism hurts:**
- Small datasets where framework overhead exceeds work
- Non-idempotent side effects amplified across threads or partitions
- Shared resources (single DB connection, single index) contend under concurrent writes

**Watch for:**
- **Multi-threaded + non-thread-safe reader** — corruption or exceptions; wrap in `SynchronizedItemStreamReader`
- **Partitioning with non-idempotent writer** — restart of a failed partition duplicates rows; UPSERT or idempotency keys required
- **Oversized grid** — thousands of tiny partitions; framework overhead dominates
- **Undersized grid** — workers idle; doesn't scale
- **Skewed partitioner** — one worker does 90% of the work; prefer hash for uniform IDs
- **Async processor returning non-thread-safe objects** — corruption in writer
- **Writer contention** — all partitions hit the same DB index; consider per-partition tables and a final merge step
- **Missing `@StepScope`** on worker step — `@Value("#{stepExecutionContext['x']}")` resolves to null at context load

**Tuning guidance:**
- Start with grid size = number of cores on the worker host
- Match thread pool size to I/O bandwidth, not CPU cores, for I/O-bound work
- For async processor: pool size ~= concurrent I/O ops (≈ 2 × RTT × throughput)
- Monitor DB load — partitioning heavy inserts can hammer a single primary

**Production example — nightly reporting ETL**
- 40M rows; local partitioning, grid size 40, thread pool 20
- Partitioner: `hash(customer_id) mod 40`
- Worker: chunk 500, `JdbcBatchItemWriter`
- Result: 6 minutes (down from 90 minutes single-threaded)
- Read from replica, write to primary
- Restart only re-runs failed partitions

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Four strategies** — multi-threaded step, parallel steps, async processor/writer, partitioning.
- **Multi-threaded step** — shared reader/writer must be thread-safe; weakens restart.
- **Parallel steps (split)** — independent DAG branches; each has its own reader/writer.
- **Async processor/writer** — processor on thread pool; reader stays serial; great for per-item I/O.
- **Partitioning** — master splits input; worker steps run per slice; best scalability and restart semantics.
- **Local vs remote partitioning** — local in one JVM, remote on separate JVMs via messaging.
- **Grid size vs thread pool size** — partitions created vs concurrent workers; can differ.
- **Idempotency is non-negotiable** — failed partitions re-run; processors and writers must tolerate it.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Batch has four parallelism strategies, and the right one depends on where the bottleneck is.

**Multi-threaded step:**
- One step, multiple threads share reader/writer
- Reader must be thread-safe — wrap in `SynchronizedItemStreamReader`
- Restart semantics weaken — `ExecutionContext` position imprecise
- Use for I/O-bound steps where restart-order isn't critical

**Parallel steps via split:**
- Independent steps run concurrently using a `TaskExecutor`
- Each step has its own reader/writer — no thread-safety issues
- Each has independent restart state
- Use for genuinely independent workloads (loading reference tables in parallel)

**Async processor/writer:**
- `AsyncItemProcessor` wraps the processor in a `Future` on a thread pool
- `AsyncItemWriter` unwraps the futures and writes actual results
- Reader stays single-threaded — no thread-safety issues
- Use when the processor is I/O-bound (HTTP calls, external lookups)

**Partitioning:**
- Master step splits input via `Partitioner` into N slices
- Each slice runs as an independent worker step with its own reader/writer
- Local partitioning — workers in one JVM via `TaskExecutor`
- Remote partitioning — workers on separate JVMs via Kafka, AMQP, JMS messaging
- Worker step must be `@StepScope` to receive partition context via `@Value("#{stepExecutionContext['x']}")`
- Best scalability + restart semantics — failed partitions restart independently

**Decision framework:**
- Bottleneck in processor (per-item I/O) → async processor/writer
- Multiple independent workloads → parallel steps
- Huge dataset that splits naturally → partitioning
- Simple single-machine, restart not critical → multi-threaded
- None fit or small dataset → stay single-threaded; tune chunk size and writer choice first

**Pitfalls to call out:**
- Multi-threaded + non-thread-safe reader — corruption
- Partitioning + non-idempotent writer — duplicates on restart
- Oversized/undersized grid — framework overhead or idle workers
- Skewed partitioner — one worker does 90% of work; prefer hash for uniformity
- Writer contention on a single DB index — all partitions serialize on the same lock

In an interview I'd emphasize that you measure first, then pick the strategy. Multi-threaded step is rarely the right answer in 2026 — async or partitioning almost always beat it on both performance and correctness.

questions.question: How do you design a remote partitioning topology in Spring Batch using Kafka or AMQP? What are the failure modes and how do you handle restart?
questions.title: Remote Partitioning Design — Kafka, AMQP, Failure Modes, Restart
questions.direct_answer: Remote partitioning uses **Spring Batch Integration's `MessageChannelPartitionHandler`** to publish `StepExecutionRequest` messages to a queue (Kafka, RabbitMQ, JMS); worker JVMs subscribe, execute the worker step against their slice's `ExecutionContext`, and reply with `StepExecution` status. The master polls or listens for replies and aggregates outcomes. Critical design choices are **at-least-once message delivery** (workers must be idempotent), **per-partition timeout** (master must declare a partition failed if no reply arrives), **dead-letter handling** (poison messages from worker JVM crashes), and **JobRepository sharing** so the master can read worker step status from the BATCH_* tables.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming Kafka delivery is exactly-once or that workers can be stateful across messages
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss JobRepository as the source of truth, worker idempotency requirements, partition timeout handling, and the failover model when worker JVMs crash mid-step

sections.title: Remote Partitioning Is a Distributed Batch Pattern Built on Messaging
sections.content:
Local partitioning maxes out at one JVM's CPU and memory. **Remote partitioning** scales across JVMs by treating workers as independent processes coordinated by messaging.

**The components:**
- **Master step** — runs the `Partitioner`, publishes `StepExecutionRequest` per slice, waits for replies, aggregates results
- **Message channel** — Kafka, RabbitMQ, JMS, ActiveMQ; carries requests and replies
- **Worker JVMs** — subscribe to the request channel, execute the worker step against their slice, publish reply to the master
- **Shared JobRepository** — the BATCH_* tables in a database accessible to both master and workers; this is the source of truth for step status

**Why messaging instead of in-memory coordination:**
- Workers can run on separate hosts (Kubernetes pods, dedicated VMs)
- Failures are isolated — a worker crash does not take down the master
- Horizontal scaling — add more worker pods to increase throughput
- Workers can be heterogeneous — some on GPU nodes, some on high-memory nodes

**The hard parts:**
- **At-least-once delivery** — Kafka, RabbitMQ both deliver at-least-once; workers must be idempotent
- **Partition timeout** — if a worker JVM crashes between accepting the request and replying, the master must declare the partition failed and restart it
- **Restart correctness** — on job restart, only failed partitions re-run; the JobRepository tracks each partition's `StepExecution` status independently

sections.title: Wiring Remote Partitioning with Kafka
Failure Modes and How the Topology Handles Them
sections.content:
Distributed systems fail in ways local systems don't. Anticipate the failure modes upfront.

**Worker JVM crashes after accepting the request**
- The worker started processing but did not reply
- Master's partition timeout expires; partition marked FAILED in JobRepository
- On job restart, only this partition re-runs (other completed partitions skipped)
- Workers must be idempotent — partial commits before crash will be re-processed

**Worker JVM crashes mid-chunk**
- The chunk transaction rolled back — no partial writes
- StepExecution status remains STARTED in the repo until timeout
- A separate "stuck step" cleanup job marks abandoned executions FAILED

**Reply message lost (Kafka rebalance, network blip)**
- Worker completed, reply went unacknowledged
- Master's partition timeout expires
- Master falls back to JobRepository — reads the worker's StepExecution status
- If status is COMPLETED, partition succeeds despite missing reply

**Duplicate request delivery (at-least-once)**
- Kafka may redeliver if worker crashed between processing and ack
- The repeat worker creates a new StepExecution for the same partition (different `JobExecution.id`)
- Worker must check the JobRepository before processing — if a previous StepExecution for this partition is COMPLETED, skip
- Or write idempotent business logic — UPSERT, idempotency keys

**Partition timeout too short**
- Master declares partition FAILED while worker still processing
- On restart, the partition runs again — wasted work and possible double-write if not idempotent
- Set timeout based on p99 partition duration, not p50

**Master JVM crashes**
- Job execution status stays STARTED in repo
- A separate operational job marks abandoned JobExecutions FAILED after a configurable timeout
- Restart launches a new JobExecution; partitions that completed are skipped

**Kafka topic partition assignment changes mid-job**
- Worker is rebalanced away from a partition mid-step
- The work is re-delivered to another consumer
- Same idempotency requirement

**Operational hardening**
- Dead-letter topic for poison messages — workers that fail repeatedly publish to a DLQ
- Replay from JobRepository — operational tool that re-publishes requests for FAILED partitions
- Monitoring on partition durations — outliers indicate skew or worker problems
- Circuit breaker on the master — if N consecutive partition timeouts, halt the job and alert

sections.title: Restart, Idempotency, and Operational Patterns
Local vs Remote Partitioning Trade-offs
sections.content:
Pick the simplest topology that meets the throughput requirement.

| Aspect | Local Partitioning | Remote Partitioning |
|---|---|---|
| Scaling unit | One JVM's threads | N worker JVMs |
| Throughput ceiling | Host CPU and memory | Cluster size |
| Failure isolation | Worker crash = JVM crash | Worker crash isolated |
| Coordination | `TaskExecutor` (in-memory) | Messaging (Kafka, AMQP, JMS) |
| Operational complexity | Low | High (DLQ, cleanup, monitoring) |
| Idempotency requirement | Yes | Yes (more critical due to redelivery) |
| Restart granularity | Per partition | Per partition |

sections.title: When Remote Partitioning Earns Its Complexity
sections.content:
**When remote partitioning helps:**
- Datasets too large for one JVM (>10M rows or memory-intensive processing)
- Workloads needing heterogeneous worker hosts (GPU, high-memory)
- Burst workloads on Kubernetes — scale workers up for the job, scale down after
- Multi-tenant batch systems where tenants run on isolated workers

**When remote partitioning hurts:**
- Datasets that fit in one JVM — local partitioning is simpler and faster
- Teams without messaging operational expertise — Kafka/AMQP infrastructure is a major dependency
- Jobs with low fault tolerance — distributed coordination adds failure modes
- Short-running jobs — startup overhead dominates

**Watch for:**
- **Non-idempotent writers** — at-least-once delivery means duplicate runs of the same partition
- **Partition timeout too short** — causes premature failure declaration
- **Master JVM as single point of failure** — implement master cleanup job
- **Missing dead-letter topic** — poison partitions block the topic
- **JobRepository contention** — many workers writing to BATCH_* tables; size the DB connection pool
- **Messaging schema drift** — `StepExecutionRequest` payload changes break in-flight workers
- **Worker version skew** — old worker code processing new partition contexts; schema-version the context

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`MessageChannelPartitionHandler`** wires the master to a messaging channel; workers subscribe and reply.
- **Shared JobRepository** is the source of truth for partition status — master falls back to it when reply messages are lost.
- **At-least-once delivery** — workers must be idempotent; UPSERT, idempotency keys, outbox patterns.
- **Partition timeout** — set on p99 duration; too short causes premature failure declaration.
- **Master JVM crash recovery** — separate cleanup job marks abandoned executions FAILED.
- **Restart re-runs only failed partitions** — JobRepository tracks each partition independently.
- **Dead-letter topic** for poison partitions — operators replay after fixing root cause.
- **Workers must be `@StepScope`** to receive partition context via `@Value("#{stepExecutionContext['x']}")`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Remote partitioning scales Spring Batch beyond one JVM by treating workers as independent processes coordinated by messaging.

**The components:**
- Master step runs the `Partitioner` and `MessageChannelPartitionHandler`; publishes `StepExecutionRequest` per slice to the messaging channel; waits for replies
- Worker JVMs subscribe to the request channel; execute the worker step against their slice's `ExecutionContext`; reply with `StepExecution` status
- Shared JobRepository (BATCH_* tables) is the source of truth — master falls back to it when reply messages are lost

**Critical design choices:**
- **At-least-once delivery** — Kafka, RabbitMQ both deliver at-least-once; workers must be idempotent (UPSERT, idempotency keys, outbox)
- **Partition timeout** — master must declare a partition failed if no reply arrives; set on p99 duration not p50
- **Dead-letter topic** for poison partitions; operator replays after fixing
- **JobRepository sharing** so master can read worker step status from the BATCH_* tables when messaging fails

**Failure modes:**
- Worker crashes after accepting request — partition timeout fires; marked FAILED; restart re-runs only this partition
- Reply message lost — master falls back to JobRepository; if StepExecution is COMPLETED, partition succeeds
- Duplicate delivery — repeat worker creates new StepExecution; idempotent business logic prevents corruption
- Master JVM crash — separate cleanup job marks abandoned executions FAILED after threshold

**Restart semantics:**
- Failed `JobExecution` retains all StepExecutions in the repo
- Restart launches new `JobExecution` for same `JobInstance`
- Only FAILED partition StepExecutions get re-published
- Workers process re-delivered slices from scratch — idempotency mandatory

**When to use remote vs local:**
- Datasets that fit in one JVM — local partitioning is simpler
- More than 10M rows or heterogeneous worker hosts — remote partitioning earns its complexity
- Teams without Kafka/AMQP expertise — local partitioning first

In an interview I'd emphasize the JobRepository as source of truth and the at-least-once idempotency requirement — those are the two pieces that distinguish a working topology from a broken one.
